articles.title: US reading scores hit near-25-year low in latest global assessment
articles.summary: Scores among US 15-year-olds dropped 14 points from 2022, as the Trump administration pushes for ‘school choice’.
articles.body:
Reading scores among 15-year-olds in the United States have fallen to the lowest level in about 25 years, according to an international education assessment.

On Tuesday, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released findings from the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), a global metric for educational achievement.

The results showed that US reading scores fell 14 points from 2022, the last time PISA results were released.

The decline was part of a broader international trend, with an OECD average from 23 countries also dropping 16 points.

But the US stood out for the size of its performance gap. Some 25.7 percent of US students were ranked as low performers in reading, while 13.3 percent were flagged as top performers.

“Looking across all 90 participating countries, there was not a single country with significantly wider inequality in reading scores than the US,” Michael Kieffer, a professor of literacy education at New York University, told Al Jazeera. “What is clear is that we are under-serving many students.”

The PISA results come as the administration of US President Donald Trump seeks to reshape the federal government’s role in education.

In March 2025, Trump issued an executive order calling on Education Secretary Linda McMahon to begin the process of dismantling the Department of Education, a federal agency that tracks student achievement, distributes federal education funds and enforces civil rights in schools.

The Education Department, however, does not establish school curriculums or academic standards. That responsibility has traditionally fallen to state and local authorities.

Still, Trump pointed to slipping test scores as a reason to shutter the department. He has also denounced the department for its “entrenched bureaucracy” and called for its responsibilities to be redistributed to the states.

In response to a request for comment on Tuesday, McMahon sent a statement to Al Jazeera echoing Trump’s push.

“The United States of America is a nation built to lead the world, yet our one-size-fits-all federal education bureaucracy has shortchanged our children and stifled our future,” McMahon wrote.

The White House has argued that federal education spending is excessive and has failed to translate into higher standardised test scores.

Since the Education Department was founded in 1979, it has spent more than $3 trillion, according to the White House.

“This moment is a stress test for our nation’s future,” McMahon said in her statement to Al Jazeera. “To pass it, we must enact a hard reset that stops protecting a failed status quo and instead builds a system that empowers state leaders and embraces innovative learning options through school choice.”

“School choice” has been a rallying cry for many US conservatives. The term refers to the practice of diverting taxpayer money away from public education to help parents finance alternative choices for their child’s schooling, like charter schools, homeschooling or private institutions.

The practice is controversial. Critics have accused the “school choice” system of weakening public education in favour of less regulated school systems that receive money with little oversight.

But since returning to office in 2025, Trump has embraced “school choice” as a form of “educational freedom”.

Last year, the Education Department announced $500m for its Charter School Program, touting the funds as the “largest investment” the initiative has ever received.

The money was earmarked to allow states to expand their charter school systems and fund new charter-school developers.

In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act – Trump’s signature piece of legislation – also created the first federal tax credit for donations to organisations that provide scholarships for primary and secondary school students, including for private-school tuition and tutoring.

Last month, Trump hosted a “school choice”-themed event at the White House to kick off the start of the new school year.

But critics warn that greater investment in education is needed across the board to reverse diminishing test scores.

“PISA 2025 shows that reversing declines in student performance is urgent,” OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann said in a statement.

“The most successful education systems focus on fewer areas in greater depth, invest in teachers, engage parents and provide targeted support for the students and schools that need it the most.”

articles.title: Trump says firefighters near ground zero carried him to safety ‘right after’ 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: Trump, who said that he was “down there right after this happened,” later said on Truth Social that he wasn’t at the World Trade Center “on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter.”
articles.body: WASHINGTON — At an event ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, President Donald Trump told a story Tuesday in which he said two firefighters picked him up off the ground near the U.S. Steel Building close to ground zero “right after” the terrorist attacks and whisked him away because they thought the building was going to collapse on them. “I’ll never forget two firemen, we thought it was coming down on top of us, and two firemen, big, strong guys. And I’m not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arm, said, ‘Got to get out of here,’” Trump said, without specifying exactly when the incident occurred. “They literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do. I’m big. They lifted me up, and they started running with me. I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself.’ But they were amazing. But they thought it was coming down,” he added. Trump, who said in his remarks that he was “down there right after this happened,” later said on Truth Social that he was not at the World Trade Center “on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter.” “Everything I said was exactly accurate,” he said of his remarks at the Ellipse outside the White House, sharing a TV news clip of him speaking after the attacks. Asked for more clarity about Trump’s timeline and actions following 9/11, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said he “was relaying his experience of a city reeling immediately after and in the days and weeks after the horrific attacks.” Trump has told the firefighter story at least once before, during a January 2016 campaign stop in New Hampshire. He has spoken many times about what he saw on Sept. 11, 2001, and his actions in the immediate aftermath. Here’s a look back at what he has said, much of which has not been independently verified. August 2026: Seeing the second plane hit In an interview with Fox News host Trey Gowdy, which aired in part Sunday, Trump said he watched as the second plane hit the South Tower of the World Trade Center. “I’m watching, and I saw the second plane hit, and you saw that come, and you’re watching it, and it’s — because I watched the air patterns for years, and you, you know, you know where the planes are. They go up right up the Hudson River. This thing was coming right into the second building. And I said, ‘Wow!’ So I watched that happen,” Trump said in the interview, shortly after he said he watched the scene unfold from his midtown apartment. Trump also said he went down to ground zero on Sept. 12, telling Gowdy he “worked long and hard” with a team of construction workers to help at the scene. “I was building a building in New York, and I had a lot of construction workers. And I went down there very shortly thereafter. The following day — you couldn’t go down the same day, but, like, the following day, very, very quickly afterwards. And we worked long and hard, but it was just so terrible and so hopeless,” he said. April 2016: Sifting through rubble At a campaign rally in Buffalo, New York, Trump said he helped clear rubble after the attacks. Trump was talking about “New York values,” speaking about restaurants and businesses that stayed open to help first responders and others in need. “These people were going through terror, and you know what happened? Everyone who helped clear the rubble — and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit,” Trump said, adding, “You didn’t know what was gonna come down on all of us.” November 2015: Witnessing people jump Trump said at a Nov. 23, 2015, campaign rally in Columbus, Ohio, that he saw people jump out of the twin towers from a window in his apartment. Trump Tower, where Trump lived at the time, is four miles from ground zero. “Many people jumped, and I witnessed it, I watched that. I have a view — a view in my apartment that was specifically aimed at the World Trade Center. And I watched those people jump, and I watched the second plane hit. ... I saw the second plane hit the building, and I said, ‘Wow that’s unbelievable,’” he said. He had told a local news station in a phone interview on Sept. 11, 2001, that he had spoken to someone that day who witnessed “at least 10 people” jumping out of the twin towers. November 2015: Watching people cheer Trump fed into a conspiracy theory that “thousands” of people cheered in New Jersey as the twin towers fell, telling supporters at a Nov. 21, 2015, campaign rally in Birmingham, Alabama, that he witnessed celebrations in Jersey City. “I watched in Jersey City, New Jersey, where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down. Thousands of people were cheering,” Trump said. He told George Stephanopoulos on ABC’s “This Week” in November 2015, “There were people that were cheering on the other side of New Jersey, where you have large Arab populations.” “They were cheering as the World Trade Center came down. I know it might be not politically correct for you to talk about it, but there were people cheering as that building came down — as those buildings came down — and that tells you something. It was well covered at the time.” There is no evidence that thousands of people celebrated in New Jersey following the attack. Local police debunked rumors at the time that people cheered.

Sullivan’s platform includes cracking down on what she described as price gouging, bolstering the VA, opposing Trump’s tariffs and increasing federal investments in housing development. articles.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
articles.summary: Since beginning his second term, the US president has said he wanted to use the word 'America' to rename a lake, a gulf and even a US state.
articles.body:
The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.

"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.

Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.

The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.

The official name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.

"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.

Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.

But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.

A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.

In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.

Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.

And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.

Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.

During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan .

After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."

The new season of South Park will premiere on 16 September.

articles.title: Appeals court upholds order blocking IRS from sharing taxpayer data with ICE
articles.summary: A federal appeals court upheld an injunction blocking the IRS from sharing taxpayer information with ICE, ruling the policy violated tax confidentiality laws.
articles.body: A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld an injunction blocking the Internal Revenue Service from sharing personal information such as the addresses of taxpayers with immigration authorities, ruling the Trump administration's policy was unlawful. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found that the IRS unlawfully disclosed taxpayer information in response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement's request for the last known addresses of 1.28 million suspected illegal migrants. The court said the IRS failed to ensure that ICE's requests met the "stringent conditions" required under a federal tax-confidentiality law adopted in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal, which generally bars the IRS from sharing tax-return information with other federal agencies. Last year, the IRS shared roughly 47,000 taxpayer addresses with ICE under a policy that aims to assist President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. The IRS had adopted a policy that allowed ICE to collect taxpayer information, sparking lawsuits over allegations that the practice was unlawful. A lower-court judge sided with the plaintiffs and blocked the policy, although by that time the IRS had already shared 47,289 taxpayer records with ICE. IRS ERRONEOUSLY SHARED CONFIDENTIAL IMMIGRANT TAXPAYER DATA WITH DHS: COURT FILING The administration appealed, arguing the ruling hindered federal law enforcement. "But that's a gripe with Congress, not the court," U.S. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard said in the appeals court's ruling on Tuesday. Pillard said the IRS procedures violated federal law in several ways, including "most egregiously" by not requiring ICE to provide an actual taxpayer address, as the law requires. "The IRS failed to require ICE to provide a 'specific reason' why the requested return information 'is or may be relevant to [a qualifying] proceeding or investigation,' as the statute demands," Pillard wrote. "It entirely fails to ensure that ICE lists a federal employee, let alone one ‘personally and directly engaged’ in a qualifying investigation of a particular taxpayer," Pillard continued. "That failure has serious consequences. When ICE requested information on 1.28 million taxpayers in the summer of 2025, ICE identified the same person as the point of contact for every single request." The practice "automates the review of millions of records without any individual review or any other means of ensuring compliance with the legal prerequisites to releasing each individual taxpayer's information," the judge added. The three-judge panel also ruled that information sharing would violate privacy laws. By providing a distinct, automated pathway for ICE to request noncitizens’ information, the Data-Exchange Procedure deprives noncitizens of the protections that section 6103 guarantees to all taxpayers," the court found. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to Reuters that it disagrees with the ruling and "will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal." articles.title: Trump gave $45,000 holiday gifts to Natalie Harp and two other White House aides
articles.summary: President Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration. The gifts of $45,000 each to executive assistant Natalie Harp, communications adviser Margo Martin, and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris as well as a $20,000 gift for director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta were noted in the staffers’ annual financial disclosure forms that were published by the administration last week. Harp, Martin and Harris make $150,000 annually and Nauta is paid $175,000 a year, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress. A White House official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Trump “has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.” The official did not say if any other staffers were given similar gifts from the president, but added that the cash gifts were not related to the “individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.” The disclosures of the gifts were first reported on Tuesday by The Washington Post. Harp is a constant presence by Trump’s side and is known for carrying a portable printer with her so she can print out favorable media coverage and social media posts for the president, who prefers reading important information on paper rather than on a screen. Martin has been working for Trump since his first go-around in the White House. She started in the first term as a White House press assistant and followed the president to Palm Beach, Florida, to help run his media operations after he lost the 2020 election to Democrat Joe Biden. She returned to the White House with Trump after his 2024 victory. Earlier this year, Trump appointed Harris to serve on the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, which has oversight over the president’s White House ballroom project. Nauta, who previously served as a valet to Trump, and Mar-a-Lago property manager Carlos De Oliveira were charged in 2023 with conspiring with Trump to obstruct an FBI investigation into classified documents that the Republican took with him when he left the White House after his first term. The charges were dismissed in 2024.

articles.title: Can the 'best showman in politics' deliver again? GOP bets on Trump at historic midterm convention
articles.summary: Donald Trump headlines the first-ever GOP midterm convention in Dallas, aiming to energize low-propensity MAGA voters ahead of key 2026 races.
articles.body: DALLAS — The stakes couldn’t be much higher for President Donald Trump and Republicans. With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — Trump and the GOP descend on Texas starting Wednesday for the party’s first-ever midterm convention, as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress. The GOP's playbook for the convention, which comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities, is to energize the party's base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress. "We are putting the president on the ballot," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters emphasized in a Fox News Digital interview on the eve of the gathering. "That's exactly what we're doing with this midterm convention." FIRST ON FOX: WHO'S SPEAKING - AND WHEN - AT THE GOP'S HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION Democrats and Republicans traditionally hold large nominating conventions during presidential election years. However, Trump a year ago floated the idea of a similar gathering ahead of the midterms, to showcase the signature policy achievements he and the Republicans in Congress produced since he returned to the White House. But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot. The GOP's solution: Hold what's been touted as a "Trumpapalooza." "We have the best showman in politics in President Donald J. Trump," Gruters said. "He is the best vote getter for these little propensity voters. He's done it three times. He's going to deliver once again." According to a speakers list, which was shared first with Fox News Digital on the eve of the convention, the president will deliver Wednesday's keynote address, which is tentatively scheduled to start at 9 p.m. ET. Trump will return on Thursday evening to the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas to close out the convention, with remarks after Vice President JD Vance gives the second night's keynote speech. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB But the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the party in power in Washington lose congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, and Trump's negative approval ratings. Gruters said, "In order to defy history, you've got to do things a little bit differently and that's why we're doing this Republican convention." "We're going to use him where we can, where it's going to be advantageous," Gruters said of Trump. "We think that this midterm convention and what we're doing over the next couple of days will be just the start of some very exciting things over the next two months." Democrats, obviously, see it differently. "Democrats are going to win back power," Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chair Ken Martin predicted last month at the party's summer meeting as he looked towards the midterms. The DNC, which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, views the GOP gathering as an opportunity to criticize Republicans. "While working families struggle to make ends meet in Donald Trump’s economy, Republicans are throwing a multi-million dollar party to celebrate Trump’s failing presidency," Martin argued in a convention eve statement. "Democrats are on the ground talking to voters about how to lower costs, expand affordable health care, and make life more affordable, offering real solutions while Republicans desperately attempt to paper over their billionaire-first agenda." Democrats have also spotlighted the sizable number of Republican politicians who are staying away from the Dallas gathering. Asked about the no-shows, Gruters said, "There's some people in tight races, they want to stay home. But listen, if you look at our speaker list, we have tons of those toss-up candidates that are here that are going to speak, that understand the value of the messaging and that we could deliver directly to the American people." Midterm elections are often a referendum on the party in power, but Republicans aim to use the convention to draw a contrast as they spotlight Democrats' leftward lurch in this year's primaries and tie the party to far-left and socialist proposals. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Gruters said speakers at the convention will ask Americans, "Do you want common sense and mainstream, or do you want the extreme left and these radicals that have been elected who fundamentally want to change our country." "They want to fundamentally change the way you live at home," Gruters claimed as he referred to the Democrats. The other part of the convention game plan is to showcase Trump's second-term achievements. "He delivered for the American worker more so than anybody has over the last five decades," Gruters claimed. "Things like the Working Family Tax Cuts, the fair trade policies, the $19 trillion in investments that you're not going to feel right now today, but you will over time. Him constantly going to bat for the American worker, Trump RX accounts... This president understands what it takes and has empathy for what people are going through." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Also boosting the GOP: Money. In the midterm battle, the RNC comes into the convention with a major campaign cash advantage over the DNC. "We've been raising a lot of money. We've been saving that money," Gruters emphasized. "Now, over the next 60 days, you're going to see us spend that money to make sure we could turn out our voters, to make sure people know exactly where our candidates stand and where the opposition stands."

articles.title: Republicans head to Dallas for first GOP midterm convention: What to know
articles.summary: The Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention kicks off in Dallas on Wednesday, a first-of-its kind event aimed at helping Republicans buck President Trump’s low approval numbers and defy historical midterm trends. The two-day event, billed by some as a “Trump-a-palooza,” will host dozens of top speakers from the administration and Republican leadership, as well…
articles.body:
The Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention kicks off in Dallas on Wednesday, a first-of-its kind event aimed at helping Republicans buck President Trump’s low approval numbers and defy historical midterm trends.

The two-day event, billed by some as a “Trump-a-palooza,” will host dozens of top speakers from the administration and Republican leadership, as well as candidates in tough midterm races. But Republicans have mixed feelings about the event, with some citing concerns about cost, timing and the potential political risk of being closely tied to the president weeks ahead of the election.

Meanwhile, Democrats are embracing the convention , hopeful that the Trump-focused event helps them draw a contrast with Republicans and get a midterm boost amid voter frustration with the president and the party in power.

Here’s what to know as the convention begins:

This week’s Dallas event marks the GOP’s first-ever midterm convention, interrupting the typical schedule of holding one every four years to mark the presidential election.

Unlike the 2024 presidential convention, when Republicans descended on Milwaukee to nominate Trump as the party’s White House pick, there’s no such official business on the docket for this two-day event.

RNC Chair Joe Greuters has cast the program as “a first-of-its-kind midterm convention that will show the American people exactly what’s at stake in November.” The event’s speakers are expected to focus on the issues shaping the midterms, from the economy and immigration to Trump’s moves abroad.

Trump, who has long floated the idea of a midterm convention, has asked his MAGA base to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot” in November, signaling his intent to make the midterms another test of his political power — and to use the convention as a way of juicing voter turnout.

Trump, who was initially slated to close out the last night of the convention, will now address the convention crowd on both days, underscoring that his record and agenda will be a major focus of the gathering.

Vance will also speak the second night, leading a speakers list chock full of other administration figures, congressional leaders and candidates in tough midterm races.

From the White House, it’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., among others.

Karoline Leavitt, who recently stepped away from her role as White House Press Secretary, will be back at the podium for remarks.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Senate Whip John Barasso (R-Wyo.) are on deck — as are Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) and Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), the respective chairs of the GOP’s Senate and House campaign arms.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R) and Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who is running for the Senate in Texas, are also among the top Lone Star State names set to speak as the event pulls major focus to tight races in the red stronghold.

All told, the RNC has announced more than 100 speakers for the two-day program. About 20,000 people are expected to attend, according to John Hiller, White House aide and the CEO of the convention’s organizing board.

Despite the star-studded speakers’ list, some lawmakers and candidates in tough races are steering clear — citing costs, conflicts and commitments on the campaign trail.

And amid a bleak midterm outlook for the GOP and lackluster approval numbers for the president, some have raised concerns that attending could even be a political risk for vulnerable Republicans.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who’s running for reelection in blue-leaning Maine, is reportedly skipping the convention — as is Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who faces Democrat Mary Peltola in a showdown that’s seen both rivals distance from mainland politics.

A Politico survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and lawmakers last week found that more than half planned to skip the event, including Reps. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.) and Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), who are battling for reelection in vital toss-up districts.

With top Lone Star State figures in attendance, the convention is set to spotlight one of the most closely watched congressional fights in the country this cycle: the fight for Senate in Texas.

Democrat James Talarico has given his party hope of notching their first statewide Texas win in decades. The state lawmaker and seminarian’s faith-driven campaign has unique appeal in the red stronghold, drawing comparisons to Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 bid, when the Democrat came within just a few points of ousting Cruz.

Decision Desk HQ’s latest polling average of the Senate race shows Talarico up by roughly 3 percentage points over Paxton, with just two months to go until the general election. The race is considered a toss-up that narrowly favors the Democrat.

Trump bucked Republicans’ Senate campaign arm when he decided to back Paxton, the controversy-laden attorney general, for Senate over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost out in a tense primary runoff.

This week, Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC funneled $10 million into Texas to support Paxton, underscoring that Republicans are playing some defense in the otherwise safe red stronghold.

Though Republicans are eager to use the convention as a way to strike a contrast with their rivals, Democrats are embracing the event as their own political opportunity.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced on Friday that a four-member House delegation would travel to Dallas to underscore the contrast between the two parties, partnering with the Texas Democratic Party on the ground.

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), a part of the delegation, in a post on the social platform X.

Multiple progressive groups, labor unions and others are planning demonstrations in Dallas on Thursday. And just before Trump takes the stage on Thursday evening, a rally is set for the steps of City Hall, organized by a dozen groups including Next Generation Action Network, Powered by the People, Texas Democrats and the AFL-CIO, according to the event page.

Talarico is also planning to counterprogram the convention with a statewide “Love Thy Neighbor” food drive, the campaign announced on Friday.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 Democrat who recently launched a new PAC aimed at helping Democrats win, is also reportedly set to stop by Dallas for remarks at a press conference.

Democratic operatives in and out of Texas have said they’re excited about the Trump focus at the convention, as they seek to tie vulnerable Republicans to Trump’s poor approval ratings and unpopular moves on the economy, immigration and foreign policy.

articles.title: Trump’s escalation of fight with Canada puts GOP Senate candidates in a vice
articles.summary: President Trump’s escalation of the trade war with Canada is coming at a bad time for Senate Republican candidates, who are being put in the awkward place of having to defend the administration’s economic record while having to push back against Trump’s targeting of critical Canadian imports and companies. Trump got pushback from a loyal…
articles.body:
President Trump’s escalation of the trade war with Canada is coming at a bad time for Senate Republican candidates, who are being put in the awkward place of having to defend the administration’s economic record while having to push back against Trump’s targeting of critical Canadian imports and companies.

Trump got pushback from a loyal Senate ally Monday when Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) called out the president’s threat to ban Bombardier, the Canadian jet maker, from selling planes in the U.S., putting hundreds of jobs in Wichita at risk.

“I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Marshall posted on X, the social media platform, Tuesday.

The Canadian aerospace company’s stock dropped more than 2 percentage points Tuesday after Trump declared it would not be able to sell planes to the U.S. market unless they build planes in the U.S. “and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’”

The vulnerable Kansas GOP incumbent spoke out after pastor Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger, accused him of being “silent” and not standing up to Trump.

“The decision to ban Bombardier from selling in the U.S. is a direct attack on Kansas workers and Kansas jobs — yet Roger Marshall is notably silent,” Hamilton posted on X Sunday.

“We cannot allow this chaotic economic policy to continue to hurt Kansans; they deserve so much better. As your Senator, I will always stand up for Kansas workers,” he vowed.

Marshall, however, tried to walk a fine line by appearing to endorse Trump’s effort to pressure Bombardier to transfer manufacturing capacity to the U.S.

“We agree on the mission: bring more good-paying manufacturing jobs back to Wichita. America buys more than half of what Bombardier sells. If that’s the market, more of those planes should be built here,” he argued, trying to temper his pushback on Trump’s threat.

Kansas’s senior Republican senator, Rep. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) also cautioned Trump against shutting Bombardier, a major employer in his home state, out of the U.S. market.

“The presence of Bombardier in Wichita supports a local workforce of more than a thousand employees, who contribute their talent and expertise to our nation’s defense and aerospace capabilities,” Moran warned.

“I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” he added.

Republican strategists say Trump’s decision to escalate the fight with Canada comes at an inconvenient moment for vulnerable GOP candidates who are trying to defend Trump’s economic record as the polls give the president poor marks on handling costs and inflation.

“Reigniting a trade war with Canada over any company is not a good idea right before the election,” said Brian Darling, a GOP strategist and former Senate aide. “You have a situation where America imports quite a few different goods from Canada, including lumber that builds houses.”

He warned that targeting Bombardier, which employs more than 3,000 employees across the country, “doesn’t make sense” because “it may end up hurting in-cycle Republicans.”

“We’re going to be looking at an election where there are some very close races and some races that weren’t expected to be close and something like this issue may become a tie-breaker,” he warned.

Kansas is one of those states where the Democratic Senate nominee is running a more competitive race than most political handicappers would have predicted at the start of the election cycle.

Marshall says he’s not taking victory for granted and predicted that Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and his allies could wind up pouring $30 million to $40 million into the Kansas Senate race.

“We’re taking nothing for granted. It’s a long time from now until November. Chuck Schumer is going to fund [my opponent] $30, $40 million,” he said.

Several recent Democratic-sponsored polls show the contest between Marshall and his Democratic opponent is a neck-and-neck race.

A Global Strategy Group poll conducted of 800 likely Kansas voters from Aug. 12 to Aug. 16 found Hamilton leading Marshall 44 percent to 43 percent. The survey, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 points, showed Marshall with a 40 percent positive job rating and 50 percent negative rating.

The non-partisan Cook Political Report still rates Kansas as a “likely” Republican win.

Marshall acknowledged that the high cost of living is a major issue in his race.

“People are absolutely locked in on the cost of living right now, despite a strong economy,” he said.

He said the cost of housing, health care, childcare and property insurance increased by 50 percent under former President Biden.

“People are absolutely struggling with the cost of living back home,” he said.

A second Republican strategist who requested anonymity to discuss the political impact of Trump’s escalation of the trade fight with Canada says the standoff with a major trading partner comes at an inopportune moment for vulnerable GOP incumbents and embattled candidates.

“With the Canadian trade war, it’s unpopular in a lot of states that touch the border,” said the strategist.

The GOP operative defended the president for trying to address what Trump and many Republicans view as inequalities in the U.S.-Canada trade relationship but warned the latest escalation with Bombardier comes at a bad time, less than two months before Election Day.

“There’s a lot of trade issues with Canada. There are in any major trading relationship. For whatever reason, this is the fight the president has chosen to champion and a lot of people who have done business with Canada are appreciative of it,” the source said.

But the strategist warned the trade fight could become a problem in several key races.

“There are obviously political considerations with Bombardier and Kansas where we’ve got a B-tier Senate race. But if everything goes sideways, everything could become an A-tier Senate race,” the strategist added.

“It’s bad for Susan Collins and it’s bad for Roger Marshall,” the source said, referring to Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough re-election race in a state that voted for former Vice President Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

The strategist said the escalation of the trade fight with Canada could also impact the Michigan Senate race — though how the issue plays out in the Wolverine State is more complicated because of the strength of unions, which traditionally have favored more protectionist policies.

Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $27.6 billion in American products on Tuesday after Trump slapped $20 billion worth of Canadian imports with 50-percent tariffs last month.

Collins, like Marshall, has been caught in the middle of Trump’s trade war with Canada, something that his given her Democratic opponent, former state Sen. Troy Jackson, political ammo.

The Maine Republican emphasized her opposition to Trump’s tariffs during a recent campaign trail appearance.

“There’s no one who has been more vocal than I have against Canadian tariffs,” she told reporters. “I voted against them on the Senate floor months ago when the president was first proposing that there be tariffs.

“I have talked to the special trade representative in Washington, Jamieson Greer, for a half hour about the exact impact on the state of Maine,” she added. “Take something like road salt, we get all of our road salt from Canada,” warning that tariffs could increase road salt costs for some small towns by as much as $10,000 a year.

Amy Fried, a professor emerita of political science at the University of Maine, said Trump’s trade war is likely to have an effect on Maine’s economy and the competitive Senate race.

“Maine and Canada have had very close relations over the years,” she said. “There’s a lot of different ways in which the Maine and the Canadian economies have intersected. It affected the lumber industry, there have been fisheries issues, a lot of tourism back and forth.”

“A lot of Maine people feel and attachment to Canada and have benefited from those relationships and Sen. Collins is trying to separate herself from it by saying she doesn’t approve of the tariffs but Troy Jackson is also talking about it,” she said, adding that the Democrat is trying to “tie Trump’s actions to Collins.”

“Clearly the economy in Maine is affected by tariffs,” she said, noting that Canadian tourism, a major economic driver in Maine, has dropped off during Trump’s trade war.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump’s midterm convention presents GOP candidates with stark dilemma
articles.summary: The Trump-centric Republican midterm convention that kicks off Wednesday in Dallas is putting GOP candidates in a tight spot. On one hand, there are clear arguments in favor of attending the convention and wrapping themselves metaphorically in President Trump’s flag. Most GOP candidates want Trump’s backing and his blessing. He said last week he is…
articles.body:
The Trump-centric Republican midterm convention that kicks off Wednesday in Dallas is putting GOP candidates in a tight spot.

On one hand, there are clear arguments in favor of attending the convention and wrapping themselves metaphorically in President Trump’s flag.

Most GOP candidates want Trump’s backing and his blessing. He said last week he is willing to spend between $400 million and $500 million from his political operation on the midterms. So, he plainly has the muscle to make a huge difference in tight races — or to decline to do so.

Trump also commands a far stronger allegiance than anyone else among the GOP’s base voters. Therefore, Republican candidates feeling antsy about turnout — and keenly aware of how fired up anti-Trump voters appear to be — are looking for a MAGA boost from the president and his convention.

But there is a wholly different case to be made.

Many Republican candidates are expected to stay away from the Dallas event, albeit often citing scheduling conflicts rather than overt Trump skepticism.

The reality that underpins such calculations: Candidates who tie themselves closely to Trump risk a major downside when it comes to appealing to voters in the center ground.

Trump is roughly 20 points underwater in terms of his job approval in the polling averages. He fares even worse than that on key issues like the cost of living, the economy and the war on Iran.

In the most recent Economist/YouGov poll , approval of Trump among Republican and Democratic partisans broke down predictably. But among independents, 71 percent disapproved of his performance and just 22 percent approved.

“Trump is an absolute albatross for Republicans running in tight races because he promised to focus on the economy and keep us out of foreign wars and the exact opposite has happened,” a senior Republican strategist told The Hill’s Alexander Bolton.

The should-I-stay-or-should-I-go argument has nuances, to be sure.

Some Republican insiders contend that the negatives of the association with Trump are unavoidable, regardless of whether candidates make public professions of closeness to, or distance from, the president.

Therefore, they say, the convention only offers upside, since it could energize GOP base voters who otherwise may give the elections a pass.

“Democrats are going to turn out,” GOP strategist Alex Conant warned. “Democratic enthusiasm is off the charts.”

For Republicans, Conant added, “We are going to be OK if we can turn out the base, and nobody turns out the base better than Donald Trump. There have been some polls showing some softness of Republican enthusiasm, and Trump can help unite the party.”

The president will certainly have a platform to try to do that.

He will speak on both nights of the convention. Vice President Vance is the headline speaker on the second night.

Theoretically, the event will give Trump and his staunchest allies the chance to make a positive case for him — and hope such an argument lifts Republican candidates more broadly.

These challenges don’t begin and end with Trump’s low approval ratings or polarizing personality, however.

They also encompass the fact that his ratings are lowest on the issue — cost of living — that most voters rank as their most important.

Meanwhile, the news agenda is mostly dominated by the war on Iran and an escalating trade war with Canada. Neither is popular with voters.

This does not, in itself, doom Republican candidates to defeat. But it leaves many strategists thinking the party needs to be disciplined and focused in its messaging in Dallas. Those are qualities that even some Trump fans would acknowledge are not his strengths.

Texas-based GOP strategist Brendan Steinhauser said he was confident Vance would “be very on-message and deliver good lines and well thought-out rhetoric.”

But he was, by implication, much less sure about Trump.

“Hopefully the president is on his game and thinking not just about the base but about independent voters and swing voters around the country. Whatever rhetoric he uses will get picked up around the country,” he said.

Steinhauser further argued that the importance of message discipline was especially paramount because of the salience of the cost of living issue — and the fine needle Republicans need to thread on it.

“That’s something we do not have a great message on,” he acknowledged. “That’s because when you’re the party in power, you either have to say, ‘Things aren’t that bad,’ which nobody believes; or, ‘Elect us and things will be better,’ but you’re already in power. The alternative is to say, ‘Elect the socialists and things will be even worse.’”

Trump, who regularly hits out against purported radicalism among his opponents, can be expected to make that argument, of course.

But will it be enough? Democrats insist it will not.

James Carville, in a newly posted clip from his podcast, cited Trump’s advocacy of AI and his views on the Iran war as evidence of the damage the president might cause to his party.

“The only answer that I can come up with that explains the current behavior of Donald Trump is simply this: He wants the Republicans to lose. He hates them. He wants to torture them,” Carville said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Conservatives split over Trump plan to pay stay-at-home parents
articles.summary: A new proposal from the White House to expand childcare subsidies to cover stay-at-home parents is dividing conservatives. The idea is not a new one. The rule change the administration is pushing forward that would make married stay-at-home parents eligible for federal funding has been bandied about by think tank scholars and Republicans in Congress. It’s part…
articles.body:
A new proposal from the White House to expand childcare subsidies to cover stay-at-home parents is dividing conservatives.

The idea is not a new one. The rule change the administration is pushing forward that would make married stay-at-home parents eligible for federal funding has been bandied about by think tank scholars and Republicans in Congress.

It’s part of a larger pro-natalist, pro-marriage platform that Vice President Vance has looked to make a priority for the Trump administration.

Terry Schilling, president of American Principles Project, a conservative organization focused on social issues, said the Vance wing of the party is right to focus on helping parents stay at home.

“These stay-at-home moms work very, very hard for very little recognition, and they don’t really ask for much,” Schilling said. “And what I think this program has the potential to do is help a lot of these moms see that the money that they put towards childcare and the time they spend away from their children really isn’t worth it in the grand scheme of things, in many cases.”

“I’m all for people having children. I’m also all in favor of those that choose not to have children, not having children,” said Joel Griffith of Advancing American Freedom, a think tank founded by former Vice President Mike Pence.

“I don’t believe that we should be using the tax code to sway people’s decisions one way or the other, to penalize people for having more children, or to incentivize people to have more children. That is not the purpose of the tax code,” he said.

The debate falls along familiar lines: the populist “new right” that doesn’t mind government intervention to bring about social and cultural change, and the more “establishment” Republican view which favors limited government that leaves such choices up to individual families.

Debate between those sides about the childcare proposal — which blew up online over the weekend — is a microcosm of the coming policy fight over what it means to be conservative, some say.

“Conservatism was sort of carrying on a tradition of [former President] Ronald Reagan for a long time, even into, you know, almost 30 years after he left office, and [President] Trump came in and blew up that consensus of what conservatism meant. How should we be, you know, what should we think about trade? What should we think about the government’s role in our lives? What should we think about reforming entitlements and deficits and all of that?” said Tim Carney, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

“I think this particular policy provides a good time to hash out some bigger questions,” he added.

The White House proposal, as drafted, would essentially expand an existing program designed to provide federal funds for single parents to pay for childcare if they wanted to work. It was part of welfare reform in the 1990s, a push to get more people off of the welfare rolls and into the workforce, and to encourage single parents — predominantly women — to pursue work or school.

The pitch then was that the federal government would subsidize childcare for eligible (usually low-income) families, typically by providing vouchers to the families or grants to childcare providers.

Now, the Trump administration is proposing changing that rule to allow families with married parents where one works and one stays at home to qualify for those funds. The move is only in a draft stage, according to The New York Times, which first reported on the project.

Key drivers of policy for the conservative movement have been at the forefront of rethinking how to distribute federal funding to encourage Americans to get married and have kids.

Roger Severino, vice president for domestic policy at the Heritage Foundation, was involved in crafting similar policy proposals that informed the White House’s draft. Severino said the goal is to level the playing field in a system that currently over-rewards families for having two working parents.

“Parents who hand their kids to commercial day care get subsidy payments, while parents who bear the toil, expense, and opportunity cost of raising their kids at home currently get ZERO,” Severino wrote on social media .

He also pointed out that the policy favors married parents because that structure is proven to give children stronger outcomes.

“Critically, the stay-at-home benefit for two-parent households would be specifically tied to marriage because of course it should. Our government provides better treatment to marriage all over law and policy because marriage, on average, provides better treatment to kids.”

The Heritage Foundation has been a cradle of such family-centered policy for decades now. But even experts there diverged over whether such a program to incentivize stay-at-home families was the right path forward, reflecting a larger dispute within the organization and the conservative ecosystem at large in recent years about the direction of “conservatism” more broadly.

Griffith was an economic policy research fellow at Heritage until the end of 2024, when he joined the Pence think tank. He told The Hill that he was part of the team at Heritage tasked with exploring economic policy ideas that could incentivize having children.

But Griffith and his colleagues — after examining other countries’ attempts to do similar things — found that such programs were often unsuccessful and expensive. Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, enacted a slew of policies throughout the 2010s aimed to reverse Hungary’s sliding birth rate, including a childcare allowance, family tax credits, loans for young married couples and tax exemptions for mothers of multiple children, among others.

That led Griffith to oppose the eventual Heritage proposal. The heart of the issue, Griffith said, is that the federal government shouldn’t be tweaking tax law to favor individual decisionmaking, like whether to stay home or work as a parent.

Beyond the political and economic argument, Griffith said he’s concerned about the social implications of paying one parent to stay home while the other works.

“We know that this is going to primarily be targeting women who choose not to work outside the home, and this could reflect a prior era in which women were discouraged not just from working but even from pursuing a higher education,” Griffith said. “This is not something policymakers should be working to discourage. This policy would discourage women from entering college and entering the workforce. And this is not a role of government. Government should stay out of those decisions.”

Other family policy experts said that the spirit of the White House proposal is the right one: making it easier for middle-class parents to stay home if they want to. In a survey conducted this year , 31 percent of parents said their ideal childcare provider is themselves, with 18 percent saying their ideal was the other parent caring for the children.

But the financial burden makes both options prohibitive. Parents who stay home instead of working lose out on the salary of a job. But putting your kids in childcare carries a hefty price tag: The average annual cost of childcare in the U.S. for two children in 2024 was $13,128, or about 10 percent of a married couple’s median income and 35 percent of single parent’s median income, according to advocacy group Child Care Aware.

“What I really like about it directionally is there is something really perverse and upsetting about saying to parents, ‘Oh, we’re really happy to help anyone but you watch your kids,’” said Leah Sargeant, an author and commentator about family policy. “That’s kind of most frustrating for parents when their kids are youngest. So, you know, the plurality of moms with really young preschool-age kids don’t really want to do official center-based care, and that’s what a lot of these programs are easiest to apply the funds to.”

Carney, at the American Enterprise Institute, told The Hill he sees merit to rebalancing any favor that the federal government has shifted toward the two-working-parent household model.

“I think there’s a lot of benefits to the model of the breadwinner and the stay-at-home mom or dad, but statistically speaking, it’s almost always a mom. And when our tax code is picking winners and losers, and it’s picking the two-income and formal childcare model, I think that’s a mistake,” Carney said. “I’m not in favor of putting all the resources of the federal government, you know, Viktor Orbán-style behind promoting my vision of the family. But I think that to the extent we have policies that sort of denigrate and discriminate against that, they should be fixed.”

But Carney and Sargeant both said this particular proposal from the White House, to expand a program designed to propel single mothers into work, is not the way to accomplish the goal.

Both floated other ideas like reforming the child tax credit, which is not a block grant and thus would not have the demand problem that the existing childcare subsidy program already has.

“Now the problem with this program is it’s already not working for the majority of families that are eligible. Only about 1 in 7 kids who are eligible to receive this money do because it’s a block grant. The money is capped,” Sergeant said. “So I think what’s kind of frustrating and challenging here is if you add more families who are eligible for this pool of limited funds, more people will miss out.”

Carney also noted that this would be an executive branch move, and he prefers Congress to be doing the lawmaking. But Republicans in the Trump-Vance wing of the party are not politically inclined to do so, he said.

“Republicans should just pass my tax reform, fold in the daycare credit to a larger child tax credit, tweak the child tax credit, allow people to claim some of it earlier, so like more of the money being concentrated up front, Congress could do that,” Carney said. “But I think part of what a lot of Trump supporters want, they actually want to bring more power into the executive, in part because they’re tired of like, ‘Let’s do things the right way,’ because a lot of Trump support is like, ‘We’ve been trying to do it the right way, and the left has been cheating. So let’s play hardball.’”

articles.body: An elected Democratic official in Michigan is rallying her community against U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and claims those within the socialist rise of her party take Black voters for granted. "It doesn't change, it's just different slave owners," Democratic Michigan state Rep. She claimed that El-Sayed is not working in the best interest of Black Michiganders and that the far-left wing of her party is "more racist than the KKK." JASMINE CROCKETT WARNS DEMOCRATS ARE TOO FOCUSED ON WHITE VOTERS, IGNORING BLACK VOTERS Whitsett called out prominent Black voices known for rallying the community's vote for Democrats — specifically naming Al Sharpton and controversial Detroit pastor Horace Sheffield III, an El-Sayed campaign surrogate. She accused the pair of working to "keep the knee on [Black voters'] neck." Whitsett said Black voters are "waking up" and are "realizing the power of our vote." "You can see the serious divide of the crazy socialist far-left and especially the White women," Whitsett said. "They are the worst and the most racist that there possibly ever could be. They're, I think, they're more racist than the KKK." "Are you trying to help the Black community or are you trying to kill it?" she rhetorically asked. "Are you trying to keep people stupid and ill-informed or what? Because right now I can't tell, right? Is this voter education or are you just trying to make sure you count your slaves on the plantation." MICHIGAN GOP LAWMAKER CASTS DOUBT ON EL-SAYED’S SOCIALIST DENIAL AS POLICIES TELL ANOTHER STORY: ‘SHARP ODDS’ El-Sayed's values aren't aligned with hers, Whitsett said, adding that she doesn't think he has the best interest of Black voters at heart, either. "I'm going to stand on Bible first, and I'm going to stand on community first," she said. I don't care about moving up within the Democratic Party. I don't care about making sure my pockets are better." El-Sayed's campaign did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment on Whitsett's criticism of the candidate and the Democratic Party's leftward shift. Whitsett is not running for re-election and will retire when her term expires at the end of the year. "I always try to be a voice of reason, and I'm not a go along, get along. So, my whole thing is it has to make sense, and I am definitely family over party. God over party is of the utmost importance," she said. "So for me, when you point that out to people, it's just common sense that to people, that's just common sense that El-Sayed is not the candidate," she continued. "There's just no way. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER "This Medicare for All, it's not for all. You're now going to put the government in your health system, and they're going to decide for you." El-Sayed already finds himself in hot water for palling around on the campaign trail with socialist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and is known for making antisemitic comments. El-Sayed has refused to condemn Piker, instead painting him as a "streamer from California" who has no bearing on the race in Michigan, despite inviting Piker to Michigan to campaign for him. articles.title: Flock cameras and TSA searches are making our 4th Amendment a dead letter
articles.summary: The natural right to privacy is a fundamental human right that government needs to respect.
articles.body:
An uprising is afoot against the Flock Safety, because its cameras had been programmed to track the license plates of drivers automatically. This is yet another example of the government treating law abiding citizens as presumptively guilty of a crime — of fishing for the guilty in a sea of innocents.

The natural right to privacy is a fundamental human right that government must respect. And the use of these cameras to monitor every movement by law-abiding citizens certainly violates the natural, God-given right to privacy recognized in the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

“The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated,” the Fourth Amendment reads. It goes on to add that “no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.”

Surveillance and tracking of all when they travel from place to place is a clear violation of every citizen’s right to privacy.

Historians recognize the importance of this provision in the Bill of Rights. The Heritage Guide to the Constitution pointed at many state constitutions that further protect this right. Virgina’s constitution, for example “declared that ‘general warrants are grievous and oppressive, and ought not to be granted.” They cited the constitutions of Maryland, Massachusetts, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Vermont, which adopted similar language.

Heritage characterized those state constitutional provisions as standing for the idea that “Warrants had to be based on cause or foundation, had to be supported by oath or affirmation, and had to name or describe the place to be searched or the persons or things to be seized.”

Flock cameras, in contrast, are a tool for conducting searches and surveillance without a warrant. One could argue that the government has issued a de facto general warrant to search all drivers of cars without any probable cause.

A handful of politicians and public officials have objected. My former boss, Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) posted on Twitter, “Flock has 120,000 cameras tracking cars across America, no warrant required. Over 5,000 police agencies have signed on. This isn’t crime fighting. This is mass surveillance of every American, and a violation of our 4th Amendment rights.”

In Utah , that Gov. Spencer Cox (R) “ordered two state entities to conduct a review and ensure that those cameras are not being misused.” In rural Missouri , the Pulaski County Sheriff’s Office stopped using the cameras, arguing that questions about constitutional rights “outweighed the benefits of Flock.” Sheriff Stacy Ball argued that “technology is important, but no piece of technology is more important than the trust of the people we serve.” These concerns are shared by most Americans.

This concern about treating all American citizens as presumptive law breakers or even terrorists is exemplified in how the Transportation Security Administration treats citizens boarding airplanes for commercial travel. Every traveler is treated as a potential terrorist, subjected to invasive screening that defies the idea that we live in a free nation. Probable cause for an invasive search is not present just because an individual purchases a ticket to travel. The more that government, both state and federal, uses de facto general warrants to treat citizens like they are all likely criminals, the less Americans feel they have any semblance of privacy.

For those who argue that those with nothing to hide should accept such searches and surveillance as a new normal, try extending that argument to privacy within one’s home or with one’s financial transactions.

Remember, the Bill of Rights are words on a piece of paper. They memorialize natural rights that all people had before we established this republic, and which they will continue to have if it ever disappears.

It is time for politicians take their oath of office seriously and dial back the Big Brother tactics to monitor citizens’ every movement. The Bill of Rights cannot be left as a dead letter.

Brian Darling is former counsel for Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.).

articles.title: BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: America’s family farms have kept us strong for 250 years
articles.summary: Round Swamp Farm in East Hampton, N.Y., traces back to John Lester 300 years ago and now anchors the new American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program.
articles.body: Half a century before America declared independence, John Lester broke soil on a 150-acre plot of land in East Hampton, New York. Little did he know, the next 300 years would see nine generations of his direct descendants cultivate that land. As our young nation took root and endured hardship, so did Round Swamp Farm. Today, Carolyn Lester Snyder carries on the family tradition by growing and selling produce on the property, with the help of her husband, children and grandchildren. They are a living, breathing, working testament to the American Dream and to America’s long legacy of family farming. This summer, the Trump administration is honoring that glorious inheritance by launching the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program. In partnership with the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture, the U.S. Department of Agriculture is building on proud traditions established during America’s bicentennial and elevating them into a unified national commitment. A long chain of uninterrupted family ownership is no small feat. That’s why this program publicly recognizes the inspirational perseverance of multigenerational farm families, from 100-year legacies to the extraordinary handful of patriots who have stewarded their land for 250 years or more. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION EXPANDS 'PRODUCT OF USA' LABEL AS PUSH FOR AMERICAN-RAISED BEEF GROWS From the Eastern Shore of Maryland to the wooded hills of western Massachusetts, from the South Fork of Long Island to the country roads of rural North Carolina, these farms remind us just how much rural America matters to all of America. Critically, they have sustained us with the food we eat and the clothes on our backs. But even more importantly, they have been the wellspring of our most cherished values and time-honored traditions. In times of tranquility and times of crisis, these men and women stand in the gap, reaffirming their commitment to the American way of life. To faith and family. To patriotism and civic responsibility. To standing where their mothers and fathers stood. And to remaining steadfast in hope for what’s on the horizon. STEVE MOORE: POLITICIANS ARE BLAMING THE WRONG VILLAIN FOR AMERICA’S RISING FOOD PRICES When the first generations of these family farmers planted the seeds of liberty, they laid the foundation for an unrivaled American agricultural might that has only grown stronger across each generation. During droughts and depression, through war and peace, their forebears kept the plows turning, the tractors running and our rich American soil fertile for freedom. These powerful legacies remind each of us that we are part of a larger story — a story we did not originally author and the ending of which we will not see. Our duty is to honor the magnificent inheritance we’ve been gifted by fighting for the prosperity of American agriculture with every fiber of our being. This is at the heart of the Farmers First agenda we are carrying out across the Trump administration. Empowered by President Donald Trump’s leadership, we are putting our farmers, ranchers and rural communities back at the center of policymaking. REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES While the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program is primarily meant to put a spotlight on farms with centuries of continuous operation, it also celebrates the future of American agriculture and the next generation of farmers who dare to take up the noble mantle of stewardship. After all, America’s success is bound up in theirs. This is what Thomas Jefferson meant when he wrote in 1785, "Cultivators of the earth are the most valuable citizens. They are the most vigorous, the most independent, the most virtuous, and they are tied to their country and wedded to its liberty and interests by the most lasting bands." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The family farms honored by the American Family Farm Legacy 250 Program are bound more closely to our nation than any others. As we continue celebrating America’s 250th birthday, it is only fitting that we salute the families whose grit, sacrifice and stewardship have fed our nation, strengthened our communities and preserved our agricultural heritage across generations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Five of those families joined us on the National Mall this summer, and we are eager to visit more in person in the coming months. President Trump has made restoring pride in America’s history a national priority, and together, we are ensuring our farmers receive the recognition and support that they deserve. articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Final major Senate matchup set ▪ GOP midterm convention kicks off ▪ Smithsonian head announces retirement ▪ Countries cut off West Bank settlements New Hampshire is emerging as a key state to watch as the primary season wraps up, with Rep. Chris Pappas clinching the Democratic nod last night to face former Sen. John E.…
articles.body:
▪ Countries cut off West Bank settlements

New Hampshire is emerging as a key state to watch as the primary season wraps up, with Rep. Chris Pappas clinching the Democratic nod last night to face former Sen. John E. Sununu (R) in the general election in November.

By most accounts, Democrats should be in a good position to keep the blue-leaning seat, which will be vacated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D), and strategists say the national mood and President Trump ’s record-low approval ratings should help Pappas.

However, in a University of New Hampshire (UNH) poll released Aug. 26, Sununu led Pappas 45 percent to 43 percent. Two months earlier, the hypothetical match-up showed Pappas leading, 47 percent to 44 percent. Both results were within the margins of error. Election forecasters Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both rate New Hampshire as lean Democrat.

Pappas’s roughly 32-point margin over progressive Karishma Manzur on Tuesday will bolster Democratic confidence heading into November. Still, as national Democrats set their sights on flipping high-profile Senate seats — including in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas — some are cautioning the party not to sleep on New Hampshire.

Democratic strategist James Demers told Morning Report that Sununu’s name carries a lot of weight in New Hampshire — both his brother, Chris Sununu , and father, John H. Sununu , are popular former governors — and the Republican Party is pouring money behind a candidate they think could have a shot at flipping the seat red.

“Democrats need to remember that the first thing and the highest priority is to maintain the seats that we already have, and New Hampshire is one of them,” Demers said.

“So, I think this should be a winnable seat for Democrats ,” he continued. “Donald Trump is polling in the low 30s here, but the Sununu name is big, and the Republican money is big, and so it could be more competitive than people think.”

Sununu has also been running as a “throwback candidate,” Saint Anselm College political science professor Christopher Galdieri said, and asking voters to “ remember when things weren’t as crazy as they are now.”

“I think that’s appealing to a decent segment of the New Hampshire electorate,” Galdieri said.

“He’s also benefited from the fact that he is not a Trumpy Republican, but he has the Trump endorsement,” he added. “ And so that sort of gives him the best of both worlds heading into the primary.”

UNH political science professor Dante Scala is skeptical the race is really as close as polls suggest.

“I’m not saying the polls are wrong, but I am saying that I don’t think that’s where we’ll be in a couple months,” he said. “I think there’s a good possibility that John Sununu has had a bit of the afterglow of his brother, who was a very popular figure as governor. I think that could be part of what’s going on in the polls.”

Scala also said the latest UNH survey suggests progressives may be holding out on Pappas, not yet willing to commit to backing him in a hypothetical match-up.

But Scala said “given the polarization” in today’s era, the idea that progressives “would not vote for Pappas over John Sununu, with the U.S. Senate control of Congress at stake, seems to me unlikely.”

Galdieri pointed to the souring national mood under unified Republican control in Washington and Democrats’ recent strong showings in polling and special elections as evidence that a GOP win in New Hampshire is not likely in the cards.

“The fact that we’re talking about potential Democratic success in places like Texas and Iowa and Ohio makes me think that New Hampshire is probably not going to be the exception, ” Galdieri noted. “ That said, I think Sununu is probably the strongest candidate Republicans could have put forward, especially in this environment.”

In the primary for the seat that Pappas is vacating, health tech entrepreneur Stefany Shaheen , the daughter of the outgoing senator, clinched the Democratic nomination over state Democratic Party Vice Chair Maura Sullivan and several other candidates.

The race between Shaheen and Sullivan, a former Obama administration official, became nasty at times as Sullivan went after Shaheen over her “fancy last name” and Shaheen slammed Sullivan over donations from people with ties to Palantir and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Shaheen will be the favorite to win in the Democratic-leaning district in November.

It’s a first ever for the Republican National Committee (RNC) and will feature plenty of Trump , along with his administration’s policies. The fate of Missouri’s congressional map is unclear after a federal judge ruled it’s too late for the state to switch back to use an old map that maintained the status quo. The ruling came after Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh in a separate case declined to lift a block on the new map, which would likely net the GOP another House seat in November.

An appeals court panel will hear arguments today in a case over access to the abortion pill mifepristone, the latest battle over abortion rights . The case could eventually end up before the Supreme Court.

TEXAS BOUND : The president, members of his administration and various Republican congressional candidates are heading to Dallas today for the start of the first-ever GOP midterm convention.

Democrats held midterm conventions a few times in the 1970s and 1980s, and had floated their own such gathering this year before deciding against it.

Trump is set to appear both nights of the event, delivering a keynote address tonight and closing remarks tomorrow. Vice President Vance will deliver the keynote address tomorrow evening.

The event will feature more than 100 speakers and try to set a similar tone to the quadrennial presidential nomination conventions that take over national attention for several days every four years.

The speakers include members of the administration such as Attorney General Todd Blanche , Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in addition to top congressional Republicans like House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), the head of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm.

Key congressional candidates like Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who are both locked in tough Senate races, will also appear.

Trump is hoping the convention, which Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters and some other Republicans have described as a “Trump-a-palooza,” can serve as a rallying moment for the party as it faces a challenge holding onto both chambers of Congress this November.

But Republicans have expressed mixed feelings about the convention, worrying that it will tie them to the president as his approval rating has continued to drop. That’s what Democrats are hoping for as they also plan counterprogramming to hammer the GOP and draw a contrast to the party in power.
